# Email

The SMTP server and sender an app's mail goes out through, and emails of the app's own, written as React components with typed data and sent from jobs, hooks and API functions.

An app sends mail through one SMTP server: Protobase's own mail ([password reset](auth.md#password-reset)), [emailed sign-in codes](auth.md#emailed-sign-in-codes)), [invitations](auth.md#organizations)), staff sign-in notices and [mentions in comments](comments.md#mentions))) and the emails the app defines itself. Both are React components, rendered to HTML with a plain-text part beside it.

## Configuration

| Variable | |
| --- | --- |
| `PROTOBASE_SMTP_URL` | The SMTP server, credential included: `smtp://user:password@host:587` (STARTTLS when the server offers it) or `smtps://user:password@host:465` (TLS from the start). |
| `PROTOBASE_MAIL_FROM` | The sender, a plain address such as `noreply@shop.example.com`. The client greets the server with its domain; a `?name=` on the URL overrides that. |
| `PROTOBASE_APP_NAME` | Optional: the app's name, such as `Shop`, which mail clients show as the sender's name (`Shop <noreply@shop.example.com>`). [`createAuth`'s `appName`](auth.md#configuration)), when set, takes its place. Without either the sender has no name. |

Set both or neither. One without the other, a URL that is not `smtp://` or `smtps://`, or a sender that is not a plain address stops the app at startup. Without them mail is off: password reset and emailed codes are not offered, a job's `mail` is `undefined`, and sending an app's email rejects.

`protobase dev` and `protobase serve` read them from the environment or the nearest `.env`; a host passes them like `DATABASE_URL`. In development, a mail catcher such as [Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) shows what the app sends without delivering it:

```sh
docker run -d -p 8025:8025 -p 1025:1025 axllent/mailpit   # its inbox is http://localhost:8025

# .env
PROTOBASE_SMTP_URL=smtp://localhost:1025
PROTOBASE_MAIL_FROM=noreply@shop.example.com
```

A project that delivers mail another way passes a `mailer`, `{ send({ to, subject, text, html }) }`, to [`createAuth`](auth.md#password-reset)) and `startJobs`, or `mailer: false` to turn mail off whatever the environment says. A template's `send` takes one too, see [Templates](#templates).

## Protobase's own mail

The auth emails (sign-in, two-factor and sign-up codes, the note to an address that asked to sign up while it has an account, password reset, invitations and staff sign-in notices) and the email to someone a [comment mentions](comments.md#mentions)) are built with React Email's components: a heading, the message, one code or button, and a footer naming the app.

- They name the app by [`appName`](auth.md#configuration)), and link it on the origin the request came to: the footer links its home page, and the note to an address that has an account links its sign-in page.
- The plain-text part has each code on a line of its own and each link in full.
- React Email and the templates are loaded when the first auth email is sent, so an app that sends none never loads them and the server starts as fast without them.

## Templates

An email of the app's own is `defineEmail`: a name, a subject, and a React component whose props are the email's data. The components of [React Email](https://react.email) render the tables and inline styles email clients need. `@protobase/server` brings React's renderer; the project adds the components, and React for its JSX, which a project with a UI has already:

```sh
bun add react-email react
bun add -d @types/react
```

```tsx title="config/emails/repair-ready.tsx"
import { defineEmail } from '@protobase/server'
import { Body, Button, Container, Head, Heading, Html, Preview, Text } from 'react-email'

export type RepairReady = { customer: string; bike: string; number: string; url: string }

// The email's data is the component's props: `send` and `render` take exactly these.
const RepairReadyEmail = ({ customer, bike, number, url }: RepairReady) => (
  <Html lang="en">
    <Head />
    <Preview>Your {bike} is ready for pickup</Preview>
    <Body style={{ backgroundColor: '#f4f4f5', fontFamily: 'Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif' }}>
      <Container style={{ backgroundColor: '#ffffff', padding: '24px', maxWidth: '480px' }}>
        <Heading as="h1">Ready for pickup</Heading>
        <Text>Hi {customer}, your {bike} is ready. Bring repair number {number} when you come by.</Text>
        <Button href={url} style={{ backgroundColor: '#0f766e', color: '#ffffff', padding: '12px 20px', borderRadius: '6px' }}>
          See the repair
        </Button>
      </Container>
    </Body>
  </Html>
)

export const repairReady = defineEmail({
  name: 'repair-ready',
  subject: ({ bike }: RepairReady) => `Your ${bike} is ready for pickup`,
  component: RepairReadyEmail,
})
```

| `defineEmail` option | |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Names the email in errors. |
| `subject` | The subject line, or a function of the data that makes it. |
| `component` | The body, a React component of the data. It is rendered with React Email's `render` to the HTML part; the plain-text part is made from that HTML, leaving out what React Email marks to skip, such as `<Preview>`. |

The template that comes back has two methods, both typed by the component's props:

- `render(data)` gives `{ subject, html, text }` without sending anything: for a test, or to look at the result.
- `send(to, data, mailer?)` renders and sends it, through `mailer` when given (a job's `mail`), otherwise through `PROTOBASE_SMTP_URL`. It rejects when mail is off or the server refuses the message.

React and React Email's renderer are loaded on the first email rendered, not when the app starts.

## Sending

A **job** is the usual place: it runs after the write that asked for it has committed, and a message the server refuses fails the try, which is retried. Pass the job's `mail`, so a job runtime started with a mailer of its own sends through it:

```ts title="config/jobs.ts"
import { defineJob, FatalJobError } from '@protobase/server'
import { z } from 'zod'
import { repairReady } from './repair-ready'

// Enqueued by the write hook of a repair that became ready (see protobase.config.ts), so the email goes out only once
// the write has committed, and a refused message is retried.
export const emailRepairReady = defineJob({
  name: 'email-repair-ready',
  payload: z.object({ repairId: z.number() }),
  run: async ({ repairId }, { db, mail }) => {
    if (!mail) throw new FatalJobError('Mail is off: set PROTOBASE_SMTP_URL and PROTOBASE_MAIL_FROM')
    const repair = await db
      .selectFrom('repairs')
      .innerJoin('customers', 'customers.id', 'repairs.customer_id')
      .select(['repairs.number', 'repairs.bike', 'customers.name', 'customers.email'])
      .where('repairs.id', '=', repairId)
      .executeTakeFirst()
    if (!repair?.email) return
    const url = `https://bikeshop.example.com/repairs/${repair.number}`
    await repairReady.send(repair.email, { customer: repair.name, bike: repair.bike, number: repair.number, url }, mail)
  },
})
```

A **write hook** runs in the write's transaction, which may still roll back. It enqueues the job rather than sending, so the email goes out only for a write that committed:

```ts title="protobase.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from '@protobase/server'
import * as jobs from './jobs'

export default defineConfig({
  config: {},
  jobs,
  options: {
    writeHooks: [
      // The job commits with the write, or not at all: no email about a change that was rolled back.
      async (event, trx) => {
        if (event.resource.name !== 'repairs' || event.after?.status !== 'ready' || event.before?.status === 'ready') return
        await jobs.emailRepairReady.enqueue(trx, { repairId: Number(event.after.id) })
      },
    ],
  },
})
```

An **[API function](../guides/api-functions.md))** may send directly, as the answer to a request:

```ts title="functions/resend-repair-ready.ts"
import { z } from 'zod'
import { defineFunction, readJson } from '@protobase/server'
import { repairReady } from './repair-ready'

const Input = z.object({ repairId: z.number().int().positive() })

// POST /api/functions/resend-repair-ready { "repairId": 7 }: the desk sends the email again, as the answer to the request.
export default defineFunction({ roles: ['desk'] }, async (request, { records }) => {
  const { repairId } = await readJson(request, Input)
  const { record: repair } = await records.get('repairs', repairId)
  const { record: customer } = await records.get('customers', repair.customer_id as number)
  if (!customer.email) return Response.json({ sent: false, reason: 'The customer has no email address' })
  const number = repair.number as string
  await repairReady.send(customer.email as string, { customer: customer.name as string, bike: repair.bike as string, number, url: `https://bikeshop.example.com/repairs/${number}` })
  return Response.json({ sent: true })
})
```

A message is sent once per call, so a job try that sends and then fails sends again: record what was sent, and check it first.

## In a bundle

A [bundle](cli.md#the-config-module)) gets React and React Email's renderer from the serve runtime, as it gets `@protobase/server`, so an email's component and the renderer share one React and hooks such as `useContext` work. React Email's other components are inlined, though `@protobase/server` uses them too: it loads them only to send its own mail, so the runtime does not supply them. Its `<Tailwind>` component needs `tailwindcss`, which the runtime does not supply, so a served config cannot use it: style with `style` props instead.
